Hi Claire / Alex —

Thanks for the call this morning — helpful to see the ClearWave streaming demo and the multi-turn examples. Quick recap of what we captured and suggested next steps so we can run the SLO qualification workshop next week.

What we heard (you can correct me):
- Primary UX: progressive streaming for long-form responses (partial tokens visible within ~50–200 tokens)
- Target SLOs: p95 tail for short responses <= 350ms, streaming partial-start <= 400ms, total tail for long responses (end-to-end) <= 800ms
- Throughput & concurrency: steady-state 250 QPS, peak bursts to 1.2k QPS for ~5–10 min windows
- Multi-turn context: average KV cache reuse ~60% across a session

Initial cost/perf levers we'd evaluate:
- Continuous batching (micro-windowing) to reduce per-token overhead while keeping first-byte latency under the streaming partial-start SLO
- Prefix/KV caching for repeated multi-turn prompts to avoid repeated attention over identical prefixes
- Model variants: evaluate a lower-latency quantized variant for short queries and a higher-accuracy variant for long-form generation
- Quantization profiles: int8 for baseline, int4 fallback for constrained capacity; measure quality delta on your prompt set

Immediate asks from ClearWave so we can size options:
- Sample 24h traffic histogram (latency buckets, QPS by minute), and 20 representative prompts (short / medium / long)
- Any hard model exclusions (open-source licenses or internal model whitelist)
- Data residency / VPC constraints for private deployment (if applies)

Attachments: ClearWave_SLO_worksheet.xlsx (worksheet to fill traffic & prompt samples).

Proposed next steps (short):
1) You share the traffic histogram + sample prompts (clearwave ops) — by Tue 10/6
2) Redwood runs a quick qualification run and delivers a 1-page cost/latency matrix + recommended levers — by Fri 10/9
3) Technical workshop (90m) to validate tradeoffs and pick an MVP configuration — propose Tue 10/12 10:00am PT

Sean will own the follow-up workshop logistics from our side; Ben will lead the technical sizing.

Thanks — talk soon.

Alex — quick technical notes to address your two questions and surface concrete levers we can test during the qualification run: 

1) Continuous batching & first-byte latency
- We use micro-batching windows (configurable) to cluster tokens that arrive within a 5–15ms window. That reduces per-token overhead (kernel launch, memcpy) while still allowing the first generated token to be emitted quickly for streaming.
- For your streaming partial-start SLO (~400ms), we recommend starting at a 5ms window for short queries and instrumenting first-byte at p50/p95 during the run. The trade: larger windows -> better throughput/cost, smaller windows -> better FBL.

2) Quantization impact (rule-of-thumb)
- int8: ~1.6–1.9x token throughput improvement vs fp16 on typical GPUs, with minimal quality regression for many decoder-only models. Latency per-token typically decreases ~25–40% depending on kernel stack.
- int4: ~2.5–3x token throughput improvement; however quality regressions vary by prompt. Use int4 as a fallback profile for low-cost tier and validate on your critical prompt set.

3) Caching & model variants
- Prefix/KV cache: if you see ~60% reuse as mentioned, expect 30–45% per-token cost drop for multi-turn sessions, and much lower end-to-end latency for follow-up responses because attention over the cached prefix is avoided.
- Model variants: propose two variants for the workshop: redwood-lite-v2-quant (low-latency, quantized) and redwood-pro-v1 (higher-quality). We can route short queries to lite and long-form to pro with an automated fallback policy.

4) Quick cost multipliers (back-of-envelope)
- baseline fp16 pro model = 1.0x token cost
- redwood-lite int8 = ~0.65–0.7x cost, latency ~0.6–0.75x
- redwood-lite int4 = ~0.38–0.45x cost, latency ~0.45–0.6x (quality caveat)
- prefix caching when effective => additional ~30–45% reduction on multi-turn sessions

I'm attaching a short recommendations PDF that includes charts and a suggested experiment matrix: Redwood_streaming-recommendations-v1.pdf

We'll run a small A/B during the qualification run to measure first-byte and tail latencies across these levers.

Ben Carter
